d.title: A 49.2 / 50.8 split is not a rounding problem
d.caption: **If the split is not what you asked for, something decided who went where — and whatever that something is, it may also affect the outcome.** Bot filtering, redirect latency, a crash in one arm: every cause removes a *non-random* subset, which is selection bias with a count attached. **So the arms are no longer comparable and no analysis can repair it.** Use a strict alpha of 0.001, because this check runs on every experiment and investigating a real mismatch costs far less than trusting a broken test. And do not reweight — that assumes you know the mechanism, and if you knew it you would fix it.

d.title: Two opposite effects, and both look like a result on day three
d.caption: **Both are artefacts of the change itself rather than of its value, and a single pooled number hides either one.** A pure novelty effect can show a 10.8% pooled lift with no real improvement whatsoever; primacy does the reverse and makes a good change look harmful early. **The diagnostic is cheap and worth running as a matter of course: regress the daily effect on the day number and look at the slope.** If it is significant, the pooled figure is an average over periods in which the feature did different things — so report the plateau, with the pooled number alongside.

d.title: Standard errors out by a factor of three, and nothing in the output says so
d.caption: **If today's residual remembers 80% of yesterday's, the model has far less information than the row count suggests** — and the only symptom is that everything looks more significant than it is. Here the naive standard errors are three times too small, **which turns a t-statistic of 1 into an apparent 3: a null result becomes a publication.** Durbin-Watson detects it in one line, and the repair is a different variance estimator — Newey-West, or a model that states the autocorrelation explicitly — not a different regression. **The first step costs nothing: plot the residuals against time.**

d.title: Engine hits are rare in the data because engine hits are fatal
d.caption: **Among the bombers that came back, 5% had engine damage; among all bombers that flew, 25% did.** The instinct is to armour the wings, where the holes are. The correct answer is to armour the engines, **because the planes that would have shown you engine damage are the ones that did not return** — the missing data is precisely the data that changes the conclusion, and nothing in the surviving data reveals its absence. The general check is two questions: count who is missing, and ask whether their absence depends on the outcome.
